Attendees at the âSalute to America 250â event in Washington, D.C., were told to evacuate the National Mall due to thunderstorms, but are now being allowed back.

President Donald Trump insisted his much-touted July Fourth show on the National Mall would go on despite severe weather that threw the event into chaos.

It was supposed to be the largest Fourth of July celebration in recent history, featuring a record-breaking fireworks display and a speech by Trump himself.

But for all the president could control, he couldnât control the weather. Thousands of spectators had to evacuate the National Mall as lightning and dark clouds rolled over the White House toward the celebration area surrounding the Washington Monument.

Subscribers read the full story here.

Watch Trump's full remarks at the Salute to America 250 event in Washington, D.C., celebrating the nation's milestone anniversary. The president's speech was delayed as weather in the area forced those in attendance to evacuate earlier in the day.

As the fireworks show continues, itâs starting to drizzle again here in Washington. Some folks are starting to head for the exits after a very long day.

Finn Gomez / Getty Images

Applause broke out in the crowd as fireworks lit up the sky at the National Mall following Trump's address. People have their phones out, capturing the moment.

Win McNamee / Getty Images

It seems like it is in a rather concentrated area. The air already looks pretty thick with smoke in the direction of the fireworks, and the wind seems to be pushing the smoke away from the celebration.

Trump finished his speech honoring America's semiquincentennial in under 40 minutes.

The president reflected on the country's history, honored veterans and promoted the SAVE America Act during his address.

Attendees now await a fireworks show on the National Mall.

Some folks are beginning to leave the event grounds even as Trump continues to give his address at the "Salute to America" event in Washington, D.C., after an hourslong weather delay.

Finn Gomez / Getty Images

While some people are leaving, others are still going through the security checkpoints where all attendees had to re-enter after being ordered to shelter from the weather earlier this evening.

As Trump's speech continues, it appears that the security line is not moving. Some people waiting in line are signing along to Queenâs "Bohemian Rhapsody."

Still reeling from a number of key setbacks at the Supreme Court, Trump said tonight that passing legislation requiring voters IDs at the polls is necessary to keep American great.

"All voters must provide a little thing called proof of citizenship, and there will be no mail-in ballots, except for illness, disability, military deployment or travel, and you wonât have cheating on the elections anymore," he said  to some cheers from the crowd. "Itâs very simple."

Republicans in the Senate do not have enough votes to either pass the so-called SAVE America Act or kill the chamberâs rule requiring 60 senators to overcome a filibuster.

Trump tonight condemned communism in his speech, contrasting the "freedoms" of America to the "talks from communists" that he said threaten them.

"Communism is a loser, and it always will be. The communist system is the opposite of the American system, and the communist system has never worked," Trump said. "We like to stop a threat like that immediately, and before it begins, it's like a cancer, you got to cut it out, you got to cut it out fast."

The president said that America's history showed that it would "never let anyone take our freedom away."

"Won't happen, and all these talks from the communists, they haven't got a chance, not even a chance. We don't want communists in our country â never worked, and it never will work," Trump said.

The president then listed a number of freedoms promised under the Constitution.

"Unlike so many others in the world, in this country we have freedom of speech, freedom of religion, equal justice under the law," Trump said.

"You showed that tonight with one flag, and as our Declaration of Independence tells us, we are all made in the image of one almighty God, and a communist will never say that, thatâs for sure," he continued.

Trump's comments came after he warned during his address at Mount Rushmore last night that the U.S. is under threat from a "communist menace."

While he did not name any particular political figures so far tonight or last night, the president has taken aim at a number of democratic socialists who won primary races in New York last month.

Trump is speaking now to a crowd filling the National Mall after being delayed by inclement weather.

"Good evening, America. If you think that was easy, it wasn't," the president said as he began his address.

"I want to thank everybody, because they did the right thing. They saw lightning, and I said, 'There's no way. If we have to speak in front of one person at 4 o'clock in the morning, I'm going to be here. There's no way we can be deterred,'" Trump said.

A robust crowd is filtering into the National Mall as Trump is set to take the stage for his remarks honoring America's 250th birthday.

Despite the hourslong delay due to approaching severe storms, audience members who returned to the venue do not appear to be deterred and are signing and dancing along to musical performances ahead of the president's address.

Christopher Macchio performed "Ave Maria" ahead of a performance of "God Bless the U.S.A." by Lee Greenwood.

Trump can be seen inside the VIP booth on the National Mall now, speaking with First Lady Melania Trump, sons Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, and others ahead of his expected speech.

Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images

Trump's daughter Tiffany Trump, granddaughter Kai Trump and daughter-in-law Bettina Trump can also be seen in the VIP area.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin were also seen speaking with the president.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and his wife Kelly later joined the president in the VIP booth.

In a lower level of the VIP booth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are also seen in attendance.

Crowds are growing frustrated at the lack of direction and are beginning to push forward as they wait to pass through the main security checkpoint ahead of Trump's speech on the National Mall.

Joe Raedle / Getty Images

Some are getting angry at others for cutting the line, while others are just excited to see the president, who just announced he is here.

The Secret Service said earlier this evening that all attendees who evacuated the venue due to orders to shelter from approaching severe storms would have to go through security screenings again.

"The Secret Service is working to make screening as smooth as possible," the agency said in a post on X earlier tonight.

Trump has arrived at the National Mall for his planned remarks to celebrate America's semiquincentennial after thousands of attendees were ordered to shelter from approaching severe storms in D.C. earlier this evening.

"IâM HERE!!!" the president wrote in a Truth Social post at 10:16 p.m. ET, an hour after he said in a separate post that he would give his speech tonight "no matter what."

Freedom 250 said in a statement tonight that Trump is expected to give his address at 11 p.m. ET despite the inclement weather.

The National Mall has reopened after crowds sheltered due to severe weather in Washington, D.C. President Trump is expected to deliver his speech as planned. NBC Newsâ Gabe Gutierrez reports on what to expect from the "Salute to America 250" celebration.

Evacuees from the "Salute to America 250" event in Washington, D.C., came together to sing the "The Star-Spangled Banner" inside the Reagan Building as they sheltered from weather.

No amount of heat or rain could prevent people from celebrating America's 250th birthday, even after evacuation orders were issued earlier in the day.

Karen Perry from North Carolina said she fainted from the heat and was given an IV drip at a medical tent. She told staff that she wouldn't leave "until I see this," she told NBC News.

"It's 250 years of America, and I love America," she said.

A woman from Boston said she was disappointed but not surprised rain briefly put a damper on Washington's big day.

"We have ponchos. We'll be alright," she said, referring to her baby. "We'll just make do."

Trump said that he will give his July 4 remarks tonight "no matter what" as thousands of attendees in Washington, D.C., continue to shelter in place due to approaching severe storms in the area.

"Storms bring luck to whatever the occasion. They also make events a little bit more exciting!" the president wrote in a post on Truth Social. "We will wait it out, I donât care if itâs 2:00 oâclock in the morning, or in one hour from now."

"Itâs Saturday night, LETS HAVE SOME FUN, even if we are out late tonight. They say 11:00 oâclock for the speech. Who cares???" Trump wrote.

Freedom 250 spokesperson Danielle Alvarez said in a statement that the gates to the event will reopen at 9:45 pm ET "at President Donald J. Trump's direction," about two hours after thousands of attendees were directed to take shelter in nearby buildings.

âAmerica, itâs time to celebrate!" Alvarez said in the statement. "The Salute to America celebration will move forward, the President will deliver remarks at 11:00 PM, and the fireworks spectacular will follow."

Trump wrote that he would be "leaving the White House soon" in the post at 9:05 pm.

"Our great veterans, especially the old timers, many of whom are there, went through hellfire, and it didnât stop them," the president wrote. "Itâs not going to stop us either! Iâm not going to let some rain stop our 250th."

Marchers in an Independence Day parade in Gilmanton, N.H., today.Â Matt Nighswander / NBC News

People gather along Main Street in downtown Stevens Point, Wisc., to watch the parade today.Â Caitlin Shuda / USA Today Network via Reuters Connect

A woman dressed as Uncle Sam greets children during the 4th of July parade in Bristol, R.I., today.Â Joseph Prezioso / AFP via Getty Images

Concertgoers at the "One Philly: Unity Concert for America" in Philadelphia were instructed to seek shelter and evacuate the festival area as severe weather is expected to hit the city tonight.

"Due to approaching severe weather, all persons should move quickly and calmly to the nearest exit and proceed to your vehicle and protected areas outside of the festival site. Please seek shelter for your safety," an announcement said at the festival area.

The delay comes as a severe thunderstorm warning is in effect for Philadelphia and its surrounding suburbs until 9:30 p.m.

The Macy's 4th of July Fireworks Show will begin earlier than originally planned due to severe weather expected in the New York City area. NBC News' Sam Brock reports on the schedule changes.

Some festivalgoers were sheltering under a museum overhang tonight, singing patriotic tunes as rain began falling.

Authorities stopped letting people into the National Museum of African American History and Culture, with more than 1,000 sheltering outside the building and some exposed to the elements.

Some were heard singing, "God Bless America" and other patriotic songs.

People shelter outside the National Museum of African American History and Culture.Â   Tara Prindiville/NBC News

NBC News' Gary Grumbach reports from the Ronald Reagan Building in Washington, D.C., where Salute to America 250 attendees have been told to seek shelter due to inclement weather possibly striking the National Mall.

Thousands of attendees have been evacuated from the National Mall due to possible inclement weather as they waited for the "Salute to America 250" event to begin. NBC News' Gabe Gutierrez reports from outside the National Museum of African American History and Culture as it reaches capacity for sheltering guests.

All attendees â more than ten thousand at this point â are being told to seek shelter in buildings near the National Mall as thunderstorms threaten the Washington, D.C., area. Organizers have delayed the start of the "Salute to America" events.

âThe safety of our guests, performers, and staff is our top priority. Due to approaching severe storms, Freedom 250, United States Secret Service, United States Park Police, National Park Service, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, and all public safety partners are asking all guests to evacuate event grounds and seek temporary shelter in a nearby building," Freedom 250 spokesperson Danielle Alvarez said in a statement.

Joe Raedle / Getty Images

Thousands of attendees braved the blistering heat in Washington, D.C. to wait in line for the "Salute to America" festivities that are set to feature an address by Trump and a fireworks show.

Maria Komisky, who traveled from Tennessee to attend, said she came out to hear Trump speak.

âI've never heard a president speak in person, much less a sitting president," she said. "My husband loves fireworks, so heâs pretty excited about that.â

Komisky traveled with her friend, Lori Fisher, who said she expects the festivities to showcase "a lot of patriotism, a lot of fun."

"Feel like this is probably over the top celebration and we wanted to be able to see it, so we wanted to come all the way from Tennessee here," Fisher said.

Eight-year-old Luke Wilkins, joined by his mom Holli Wilkins, came to Washington from Florida to watch his father, who is in one of the jets participating in the U.S. Navy's Blue Angels' flyovers.

Asked about the heat, Luke said "it's worth it" and later added that watching his dad do flyovers was "really cool." Luke said he was also excited to see the fireworks show.

Jimmy Zumba said he traveled from Houston and waited in line for the event for about two hours today. He said that he was "waiting for a nice speech from the president, fantastic fireworks."

Despite his excitement to see Trump's address, Zumba said he thinks the event could have been coordinated better amid the sweltering temperatures. He said it was âa little unnecessary to open the doors at five when there are many people heat exhausted," and added that he thought it would have been better to open the doors sooner.Â

âI saw a few people passing out, unfortunately," Zumba said.

Jack Kowalski, who traveled from Charles City, Virginia, said that he got to the venue gate at 1 pm.

"Everybody kept crowding closer and closer and closer. By 5 oâclock there were at least four people that needed medical attention,â Kowalski said. âIf they can let us all get through and just spread us out, it would have been a whole lot better."

Valerie Plesch / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Valerie Plesch / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Valerie Plesch / Bloomberg via Getty Images

A naturalization ceremony took place today at George Washingtonâs Mount Vernon in Virginia.

Skylar Baird arrived at the National Mall at 8 a.m. today to beat the heat, she said. Originally from Tennessee, Baird said she's interning in D.C this summer and can't wait for festivities to get underway

"A lot of people have been passing out, so a lot of people are really dedicated to get here," she said of the heat.

When asked how it feels to celebrate America's 250th birthday in the capital, she said: "Amazing, great, super excited and really excited to see what's in store for tonight."

Trump will give a "historical speech" tonight to honor the country's semiquincentennial that will be "unlike any other he's given before," a senior White House official said this evening.

âThe President will give a historical speech tonight, looking back on our nationâs history since its founding 250 years ago and utilizing the stories of American heroes to tell it," the official said. "It will be a unique speech unlike any other heâs given before.â

President Trump at Mount Rushmore National Memorial in Keystone, S.D. on Friday.Â Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images

Asked whether the speech would be merely historical or veer into current politics, as Trump did by commenting on "communist threats" during his address last night at Mount Rushmore, the official said they couldn't answer definitively because of as 4:30 pm ET,  Trump had not yet reviewed tonight's speech.

Trump teased Wednesday that while it would be "approximately 107 degrees out" on July 4, he would give a "really long speech just to show that I can do anything."

Temperatures reached above 100 degrees in Washington, D.C., today, according to the National Weather Service, as spectators await the president's remarks on the National Mall.

Trump wrote in a Truth Social post this afternoon that "Despite the heat, which isnât as bad as predicted, the crowds in D.C. are INCREDIBLE!"

He wrote that he would be speaking at around 10:00 pm at the Lincoln Memorial.

Emergency medical workers provide assistance at the Great American State Fair on the National Mall on Saturday. Organizers were forced to delay its opening because of the heat.Â Joe Raedle / Getty Images

Fairgoers reach for bottled water at the entrance to the Great American State Fair on Saturday. Pallets of water bottles were seen baking in the open sun.Â Anna Rose Layden / Getty Images

An attendee uses a bag of ice to cool off along the National Mall on Saturday, where temperatures jumped over 100 degrees.Â Alexi J. Rosenfeld / Getty Images

Members of the National Guard provide assistance at the entrance to the Great American State Fair on Saturday.Â Anna Rose Layden / Getty Images

The gates to the "Salute to America" festivities in Washington, D.C., are open as of 5:22 p.m.

Trump is set to headline the event later this evening as the city continues to endure scorching heat.

Washingtonâs âSalute to America 250â celebration is expected to draw thousands to the National Mall for an evening of music, military flyovers, President Donald Trumpâs address and what organizers say will be the largest single fireworks display ever produced.

The event is also making history for another reason: It is the first Fourth of July celebration in the nationâs capital to be designated a National Special Security Event, a classification typically reserved for presidential inaugurations, Super Bowls, national political conventions and the United Nations General Assembly.

Alexi J. Rosenfeld / Getty Images

The designation puts the U.S. Secret Service in charge of security and brings together the Department of Homeland Security, the FBI, FEMA and dozens of federal, state and local agencies. More than 4,800 National Guard members from 23 states and the District of Columbia are also deployed across Washington.

Miles of security fencing now surround the National Mall, with extensive road closures and airport-style screening at entrances to both the Great American State Fair and the Salute to America event. Attendees should expect stricter security than in previous years. Items including coolers, folding chairs, frisbees, balls, metal drink containers and aerosol cans â including spray sunscreen â are prohibited.

Federal officials say they are not aware of any credible threats. During a security briefing Monday, the FBI's Washington field office Assistant Director in Charge Darren Cox said authorities were ânot tracking any credible threats.â U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro echoed that assessment Thursday.

One challenge officials could still face is the weather. With dangerous heat already affecting the region and thunderstorms possible later today, any evacuation of the National Mall could require moving thousands of people out of the secured event area on short notice.

A festive, carnival-like atmosphere has taken shape at Fort Campbell, where families are arriving for an Independence Day celebration.

Despite hot, humid conditions, a respectable crowd has already gathered, with organizers expecting attendance to grow as temperatures ease later this evening. The celebration includes carnival rides, live music, food vendors and a fireworks show honoring the nation's 250th anniversary.

There has been little relief from the afternoon sun ahead of the "Salute to America 250" celebration on the National Mall.

Megan Lebowitz Brand / NBC News

The rows of chairs facing the stage offered virtually no shade, including reserved sections for VIPs and World War II veterans. While umbrellas covered a separate seating areas, the seats closest to the stage remain fully exposed.

Megan Lebowitz Brand / NBC News

Organizers set up a large air-conditioned cooling tent with tables and chairs, along with hydration stations around the National Mall. Pallets of bottled water outside the cooling tent sat baking in the sun.

Military flyovers added to the atmosphere, with the roar of aircraft overhead loud enough to make seats visibly vibrate.

As many good stories do, this one begins in Italy.

In 1889, Constantine Vitale opened a fireworks shop in his small Italian town, turning his fascination with pyrotechnics into a family business.

When he immigrated to the United States in 1920, he brought that expertise with him. After settling in New Castle, Pennsylvania â north of Pittsburgh â he opened up a fireworks business that would eventually become Pyrotecnico.

More than a century later, the company is in its fifth generation, producing fireworks, drone and light shows for everyone from Cardi B to the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival, as well as communities across the country.

But nothing has compared to this.

âI think if he would see the company today, he would probably be incredibly proud, but probably think we were a little crazy,â Constantineâs great-grandson and current CEO Stephen Vitale told NBC News.

On July Fourth in Washington, D.C., Pyrotecnico plans to launch more than 850,000 fireworks, aiming to shatter a world record previously set by a megachurch in the Philippines a decade ago.

The 40-minute display will launch from eight barges on the Potomac River and two land-based sites â West Potomac Park and the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. In all, about 58,000 pounds of fireworks were transported from western Pennsylvania to the nationâs capital, where a crew of 75 Pyrotecnico employees will bring the show to life.

To create the display, designer Jason Farrell traveled the world in search of the right fireworks. The finale will feature shells from Spain, Italy and China.

âEach country kind of has their own take on how they create fireworks, so everybody has kind of a specialty of what they do,â Farrell said.

The fireworks will be synchronized to a live soundtrack performed by a military band made up of musicians from several branches of the U.S. armed forces. The setlist spans six decades and includes âDonât Stop Believinâ,â âCourtesy of the Red, White & Blue,â âSweet Carolineâ and âParty in the U.S.A.â

âThereâs something about the feeling and the honor of doing a firework display on the Fourth of July in Washington, D.C.,â Vitale said. âItâs Independence Day at its best.â

At least 19 "suspected heat-related deaths" have been reported in New Jersey since July 2, New Jersey's health commissioner said this afternoon.

The commissioner, Dr. Raynard Washington, said the deaths affected people in different conditions and age ranges and urged all New Jersey residents to stay safe as the heat wave continues.

Michael Nagle / Bloomberg via Getty Images

"Unfortunately, many of these individuals were found in homes without air conditioning; few were outside of their residence, some on the street, and some even in parked cars," Washington said at a press conference today. "It's important to note that the age ranges for these individuals were not just the elderly; they were folks who were younger adults."

The 19 deaths are a sharp increase from the six deaths that were reported during last yearâs heat wave, Washington said. Alongside a rise in heat-related deaths, Washington said, there has been in a spike in the number of hospital visits for heat-related illnesses across the state so far this week.

"This is not a typical summer heat wave, and it's really important that we all take it serious, because it can become life-threatening really quickly," Washington said.

"So, stay hydrated, stay cool, avoid being outside for long periods of time, and ensure that individuals that are in your neighborhood, in your community, you're checking on them. There's a role for all of us to play to help in this," he continued.

With the gates set to open in 45 minutes, dangerous heat is bearing down on the National Mall as thousands prepare to attend the "Salute to America 250" celebration.

A temperature reading taken from the thousands of chairs arranged for the attendees registered about 160 degrees, showing just how hot surfaces have become under the afternoon sun.

Cooling stations, water distribution points and misting tents have been set up around Washington Monument grounds, which are scheduled to open to the public at 5 p.m. ET.

The conditions are a stark contrast to the nation's bicentennial celebration in Washington in 1976, when the high temperature reached 84 degrees and the low dipped to 65 degrees, according to Department of Commerce data.

Organizers of the Freedom 250 celebration on the National Mall said they are closely monitoring weather conditions as severe thunderstorms threaten parts of the Washington area head of this evening's festivities.

Members of the National Guard at the Great American State Fair on Saturday.Â Finn Gomez / Getty Images

"The safety of our guests, performers, and staff is our top priority," Freedom 250 spokesperson Danielle Alvarez said in a statement. She added that Freedom 250, the U.S. Park Police, National Park Service, U.S. Secret Service, FEMA and other public safety partners are actively monitoring conditions.

Despite triple-digit heat indexes, visitors from across the country gathered in Philadelphia today to celebrate the nation's 250th birthday at the birthplace of American independence.

Jeff Wilkins, a historical re-enactor from Knoxville, Tennessee, dressed as a colonial militiaman, said attending the celebration was a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

"We're really here just celebrating a great day in our history," a visibly emotional Wilkins said. "to be part of the, you know, the nationâs birthday today. Iâm humbled."

Jeff Wilkins, a historical re-enactor from Knoxville, Tennessee.Â   NBC News

Others traveled hundreds of miles specifically to mark the anniversary where the Declaration of Independence was signed. Max and Theresa Stewart of Arlington, Texas, planned their trip around the milestone and said it was an opportunity to reflect on the sacrifices made to establish the country.

"It just needs to be observed and appreciated," Theresa Stewart said, noting her father served in the Korean War and her son served in the National Guard.

For Sharad and Seema Goyal, who drove from Washington, D.C., the day was also about sharing history with the next generation. They brought their children to see Independence Hall and the Liberty Bell before attending a World Cup match later in the day.

"Iâd like to share with them a little bit about our history," Sharad Goyal said.

Visitors said they were taking precautions against the heat by carrying water, portable fans and sunscreen, while limiting their time outdoors between events.

Despite triple-digit temperatures, attendees began lining up hours before the gates were set to open at 5 p.m. ET for the "Salute to America 250" celebration on the National Mall.

People wait in line to enter the National Mall today.Â Finn Gomez / Getty Images

The event, one of the marquee celebrations marking the nation's 250th anniversary, is expected to draw large crowds for Trump's evening address, followed by a fireworks display.

The National Weather Service issued a severe thunderstorm watch for the Washington area, which could complicate plans for fireworks displays, including the show the president will attend in Washington.

So far, there have been no announcements affecting the timing of the Washington show.

Masked men, some carrying Confederate flags, marched through Washington, D.C., today in scenes captured on social media videos.âReclaim America, reclaim America,â the crowd was heard chanting in a video captured near Union Station by local reporter Mitchell Miller, who said the group called for getting rid of immigrants.

In Millerâs video, some members of the group can be seen carrying flags that appear to depict the Patriot Front logo. The Anti-Defamation League describes Patriot Front as a white supremacist group.

Other videos on social media appear to show the group marching near the Eastern Market Metro station.

Finn Gomez, a Getty Images photographer, shared an image of people in face masks and apparent Patriot Front gear riding the Metro.

Members of the white supremacist group Patriot Front ride the Washington Metro on Saturday in Washington, D.C. Â Finn Gomez / Getty Images

Crowds gathered in the sweltering heat Saturday to celebrate the United Statesâ 250th birthday by watching famed competitive eater Joey âJawsâ Chestnut defend his world hot dog eating championship in Coney Island, where he downed 66 hot dogs in just 10 minutes. Miki Sudo defended her title as well in the womenâs division.

Saturday marked the 18th time Chestnut, 42, won the so-called Mustard Belt in just 21 appearances at the internationally televised Nathanâs Famous Fourth of July hot dog eating contest. He beat out 13 competitors who came from around the country and world, trekking from the Czech Republic, Australia and South Korea.

âItâs a dream, itâs electric, thereâs no place better on Earth,â Chestnut said breathlessly in an interview immediately after the showdown, donning a bulky, bejeweled necklace bearing the name of the sports betting company Polymarket around his neck. In a video posted on Instagram before the competition, Chestnut called competitive hot dog eating âthe most patriotic sport weâve got.â

Joey Chestnut raises his fist after winning the 2026 Nathan's Famous Fourth of July hot dog eating contest in New York City today. Â Anna Connors / AP

Chestnut handily defeated the second-place winner, Patrick Bertoletti, 41, who ate 50 hot dogs, but fell short of his own 2021 record of 76 wieners and buns â or approximately 7.6 hot dogs per minute.

Defending champion in the womenâs division, the 40-year-old Sudo of Tampa, Florida, won the bright pink Mustard Belt for the 12th time, downing 38.75 dogs. In 2024, she ate a record 51 links.

After competing, Sudo joined the crowd to watch her husband â who proposed to her in 2021 immediately after downing 50 boiled eggs in just over three minutes to set a world record â compete in the menâs event.

Both champions said that the heat wave that scorched New York on Saturday â bringing temperatures in Brooklyn to roughly 90 degrees Fahrenheit (32 degrees Celsius) during the competition â made it that much more difficult. On top of that, ESPN announcers said the humidity changed the consistency of the buns.

âI just said I would have to rely on muscle memory, and the crowd really carried me through to another belt today,â Sudo said.

A large crowd braved the heat to watch the event, wearing foam hot dogs on their heads and standing outside the original Nathanâs Famous restaurant that has been in Coney Island, Brooklyn, since 1972. The superfans who stood closest to the stage wore ponchos as protection in case a competitor threw up.

There was briefly some concern earlier this year that Chestnut wouldnât be able to participate in the 2026 competition after he was arrested for allegedly slapping a man in an Indiana bar. He was put on probation after pleading guilty to misdemeanor battery, but is allowed to travel outside Indiana. Hot dog contest organizer Major League Eating said the criminal case didnât affect Chestnutâs eligibility for the competition.

Despite his continued reign, Chestnut told an ESPN interviewer after the game that he was disappointed that he wasnât able to top his previous record.

âDang, I got so much room left,â said Chestnut, whom announcers referred to as the âMichelangelo of Mastication.â

Dangerous heat is forcing organizers across the eastern U.S. to cancel or alter Independence Day celebrations, with dozens of parades, festivals and fireworks affected as the nation marks its 250th birthday. In Pennsylvania and New Jersey alone, nearly a dozen July Fourth events have been called off or postponed because of the weather.

In a social media post, former President Joe Biden honored America's 250th anniversary, writing, "Two hundred and fifty years ago, a group of Americans signed their names to a piece of parchment and made a promise no nation had ever made before: that weâre all created equal, endowed by our Creator with unalienable rights â life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness."

He added: "We chose that path 250 years ago but thatâs where the work began, not where it ended. Every generation has had to choose it again. At Valley Forge, at Gettysburg, on the beaches of Normandy, in the streets of Selma."

"Now itâs our turn," he wrote, adding: "250 years in, we still havenât fully lived up to those words in the Declaration. But weâve never walked away from them."

"Our story isnât finished. Letâs keep writing it together," he wrote at the end.

NBC Newsâ Dylan Dreyer gives an inside look at Sail4th 250 from a boat in New York Harbor as the country celebrates Americaâs 250th birthday.

In his Annapolis speech, the Maryland governor said, "Too many watch as military conflict starts to feel like a conquest, where those who wear the uniform are asked to do the impossible, and those back home are asked to pay for the unnecessary."

The governor did not mention the Iran war by name but said: "Starting war without a purpose is not patriotic. Ending a war without achievement is not victory. And telling soldiers and sailors and airmen and Marines otherwise is not leadership."

Moore added that starting wars like this is what can "make people increasingly skeptical, and that skepticism is not unfounded. That skepticism is not unpatriotic."

In his Independence Day speech, Gov. Wes Moore, D-Md., acknowledged the need to celebrate, but also called for a "day of reflection" and spoke about his grandfather fleeing South Carolina as a boy due to the violence of the Ku Klux Klan.

"What does the work of patriotism require of us, this is a day of reverence, but it also must be a day of reflection, because the Founding Fathers knew this country was unfinished," Moore said.
